newsitem.title: CANADA: PanCanadian sees improvement in 2nd half.
newsitem.headline: PanCanadian sees improvement in 2nd half.

text.p: PanCanadian Petroleum Ltd expects in the rest of 1997 to regain oil and gas production and cash flow lost earlier this year through sales and operational problems, PanCanadian Chief Executive David Tuer said on Tuesday.
Much of the production increase, especially in crude oil, was expected to come from last month's acquisition of heavy oil producer CS Resources Ltd, Tuer said in a conference call.
Tuer said the company expected to post 1997 earnings of C$370 million and cash flow of C$970 million.
PanCanadian posted 1996 earnings of C$346 million and cash flow of C$1 billion.

Tuer said oil and gas liquids production for the year was expected to average 150,000 barrels a day, up slightly from 146,331 in 1996. He pegged natural gas output for 1997 at 770 million cubic feet a day, up from 717 million last year.

"We have changed our underlying PanCanadian forecast only slightly since the (Canadian Association of Petroleum Producers June investment conference) and have added the CS volumes for the remaining five months of the year," Tuer said.
He said the new outlook included daily production from CS of 19,000 barrels a day of crude oil and liquids and 14 million cubic feet a day of natural gas.

Tuer said the company's financial assumptions were based on an unchanged West Texas Intermediate oil price forecast of US$20 a barrel and a higher natural gas price forecast of C$1.80 per thousand cubic feet.

But the discount on heavy crude oil compared to light crude was expected to remain deep for at least the next year "and maybe two," he said, bringing the company's realized oil price down by about US$1 a barrel, he said.

Tuer said the lower production reported in the second quarter compared to the same period in 1996 -- a 12,000 barrel a day deficit -- was only partly from property sales and the rolling of its Syncrude Canada Ltd stake into a royalty trust.

PanCanadian was also hit by surface access problems caused by wet weather, high production levels at one of its oil facilities and a faulty decision to change to narrower casing on 300 heavy oil wells, which caused lower production rates.
The three problems made up for 8,500 barrels a day of the shortfall, he said.
"We didn't expect to see the dramatic shortfall we experienced," he said.
